source_text: ἀλλ᾿ ὡς καὶ προφῆται προεῖπον, ἀπὸ παρθένου. κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν σημείου γεννώσης τὸν ἐπώνυμον πράγματος, δηλοῦντος ὅτι ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει αὐτοῦ μετ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἔσται θεός. Καὶ οἰκεῖόν γε φαίνεταί μοι πρὸς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν παραθέσθαι τὴν τοῦ Ἡσαΐου προφητείαν, λέγουσαν ἐκ παρθένου τεχθήσεσθαι τὸν Ἐμμανουήλ· ἣν οὐκ ἐξέθετο, εἴτε μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος εἴτ᾿ ἀναγνοὺς μὲν ἑκὼν δὲ σιωπήσας, ἵνα μὴ δοκοίη κατασκευάζειν ἄκων τὸν λόγον ἐναντιούμενον αὐτοῦ τῇ προαιρέσει. ἔχει δ᾿ οὕτως ἡ λέξις· „καὶ προσέθετο κύριος τῷ Ἄχαζ λέγων· αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου θεοῦ σου εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος. καὶ εἶπεν Ἄχαζ· οὐ μὴ αἰτήσω οὐδ᾿ οὐ μὴ πειράσω τὸν κύριον. (καὶ εἶπεν·) ἀκούσατε δὴ, οἶκος Δαυὶδ, μὴ μικρὸν ὑμῖν ἀγῶνα παρέχειν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ πῶς κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα; διὰ τοῦτο δώσει κύριος αὐτὸς ὑμῖν σημεῖον· ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ“, ὅπερ ἑρμηνεύεται „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός“. ὅτι δὲ κακουργῶν ὁ Κέλσος οὐκ ἐξέθετο τὴν προφητείαν, δῆλόν μοι γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ παραθέμενον αὐτὸν πολλὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγελίου, ὥσπερ τὸν ἀνατείλαντα ἀστέρα ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν παραδόξων, μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν τούτου ἐμνημονευκέναι. ἐὰν δὲ Ἰουδαῖος εὑρεσιλογῶν τὸ „ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος“ μὴ γεγράφθαι λέγῃ ἀλλ᾿ ἀντ᾿ αὐτοῦ „ἰδοὺ ἡ νεᾶνις“, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι ἡ μὲν λέξις ἡ ἀαλμὰ, ἣν οἱ μὲν ἑβδομήκοντα μετειλήφασι πρὸς τὴν παρθένον ἄλλοι δ᾿ εἰς τὴν νεᾶνιν, κεῖται, ὥς φασι, καὶ ἐν τᾷ Δευτερονομίῳ ἐπὶ παρθένου, οὕτως ἔχουσα·„ἐὰν δὲ γένηται παῖς παρθένος μεμνηστευμένη ἀνδρὶ, καὶ εὑρὼν αὐτὴν ἄνθρωπος ἐν πόλει κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐξάξετε ἀμφοτέρους ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν, καὶ λιθοβοληθήσονται λίθοις, καὶ ἀποθανοῦνται· τὴν νεᾶνιν ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι οὐκ ἐβόησεν ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι ἐταπείνωσε τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ·“ καὶ ἑξῆς· „ἐὰν δὲ ἐν πεδίῳ εὕρῃ ἄνθρωπος τὴν παῖδα τὴν μεμνηστευμένην καὶ βιασάμενος αὐτὴν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, ἀποκτενεῖτε τὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν κοιμώμενον μετ᾿ αὐτῆς μόνον, καὶ τῇ νεάνιδι οὐ ποιήσετε οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔστι τῇ νεάνιδι ἁμάρτημα θανάτου.“
pass_a_gloss: But as also prophets spoke beforehand, from a virgin. According to a promise of a sign, the one giving birth to the one named after the thing, showing that God will be with men at his birth. And it seems to me to be fitting to set forth the prophecy of Isaiah in relation to the personification of the Jew, saying that Emmanuel will be born from a virgin; which Celsus did not expound, either because he did not know, although he promises to know all, or because he read it but deliberately kept silent, so that he might not seem to be constructing against his will an argument opposing his preference. The text has it thus: 'And the Lord added to Ahaz, saying, Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either into the depths or into the heights. And Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord.' And he said, 'Hear now, house of David, is it not enough for you to make people tired, and how do you make the Lord tired? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin will conceive in the womb and will give birth to a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel', which is interpreted as 'God with us'. That Celsus, acting maliciously, did not expound the prophecy is clear to me from the fact that he passed over many things from the Gospel according to Matthew, such as the star rising at the birth of Jesus and other remarkable things, and did not even mention the beginning of it. But if a Jew, seeking to find something to say, says that 'behold, the virgin' is not written but instead 'behold, the young woman', we will say to him that the phrase 'alma', which the Seventy translators rendered as 'virgin' and others as 'young woman', is also found, as they say, in Deuteronomy, concerning a virgin, having it thus: 'If a virgin betrothed to a man is found, and a man finds her in a city and lies with her, and you will bring out both of them to the gate of their city, and they will be stoned with stones, and they will die; the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he humbled the wife of his neighbor'; and next: 'If a man finds the betrothed girl in a field and the man rapes her and lies with her, you will kill the man who lay with her alone, and to the girl you will do nothing; there is no sin of death for the girl'.

pass_b_english: Just as the prophets also foretold, the Messiah would come from a virgin. This came about in fulfillment of a promised sign: the one who would give birth to the child bearing the name that embodies the reality, showing that God would be with human beings at his birth. It also seems appropriate to me, in addressing the Jew’s persona, to set forth the prophecy of Isaiah, which declares that Emmanuel will be born of a virgin—a passage that Celsus omitted. He may have omitted it because he did not know it, despite his claim to know everything, or because he read it yet deliberately kept silent, so as not to appear to be constructing against his will an argument that ran counter to his own preference. The text reads as follows: ‘And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying, “Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, whether in the depths or in the heights.” But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord.” Then he said, “Hear now, O house of David: Is it too little for you to weary men, that you also weary my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Immanuel”’ (Isaiah 7:14), which is interpreted ‘God with us’. That Celsus acted maliciously in omitting this prophecy is clear to me from the fact that he passed over many things from the Gospel according to Matthew—such as the star that rose at the birth of Jesus and other remarkable events—and did not even mention the beginning of that account (Matthew 1:23). But if a Jew, seeking something to argue, claims that ‘Behold, the virgin’ is not written but rather ‘Behold, the young woman,’ we will reply that the Hebrew word ‘almah,’ which the Seventy translators rendered as ‘virgin’ and others as ‘young woman,’ is also found, they say, in Deuteronomy concerning a virgin. The passage reads: ‘If a virgin betrothed to a man is found in the city, and a man lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city and stone them to death—the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor’s wife’ (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). And immediately afterward: ‘If a man finds a betrothed girl in the open country, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die; but you shall do nothing to the girl, for the girl has committed no offense punishable by death.’

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text, including the nuances of the debate over 'alma' vs 'neanis' and the specific legal language of Deuteronomy. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering with correct scripture citations (Isaiah 7:14, Matthew 1:23, Deuteronomy 22:23–24) that match the Greek content.
